rationale: Ambitious, well-executed mixed online/field experiments on a timely question. Strong internal validity, large sample (≈880k registered voters exposure), administrative outcomes, placebo control online, heterogeneous-effects analysis, and robustness. Some risks (spillovers across neighborhoods, opposition-only partners, framing/partisanship in basic treatment) and limited external validity temper the top score.

Core claims (misperceptions exist; accurate info shifts beliefs and opposition vote share; stronger among misinformed/government-leaning) are tightly linked to evidence. Online placebo helps separate demand effects. Field results use administrative vote shares. Claims remain measured. Caveats on generalizability are noted, though interference/spillovers are not deeply probed.

Sound design: randomized neighborhood canvassing; 2SLS using completion; strong first stages; rich controls; preregistration; robustness across instruments/controls; heterogeneity by baseline alignment. Concerns: potential spillovers between adjacent areas; only opposition parties partnered (credibility partly mitigated via non-affiliated canvassers); multiple outcomes with limited MHT adjustment; SUTVA not fully addressed.

Combines belief-correction mechanisms with large-scale electoral outcomes in an authoritarian context, advancing literatures on democratic demand, persuasion, and corruption/media. Novel joint online-placebo and field evidence; identifies who moves and under what messenger credibility. High value for researchers and practitioners designing pro-democracy interventions.

Clear articulation of questions, hypotheses, treatments, and outcomes. Transparent exposition of bundled/unbundled analyses, heterogeneity, and robustness. Figures and appendices aid interpretation. Minor gaps: limited discussion of potential geographic spillovers and formal MHT handling.

IRB approvals, AEA RCT registry (AEARCTR-0011480), and detailed online supplement signal good practices. Administrative YSK data are public. It’s unclear if full anonymized microdata and code for both experiments are openly available, which constrains full reproducibility.

Highly relevant to global priorities: democratic resilience, combating authoritarian misinformation, and practical electoral interventions. Provides actionable effect sizes (≈2–4 pp vote-share shifts) and guidance on messenger credibility. Insights plausibly generalize to similar regimes, albeit with contextual caveats.

Agenda-setting theory paper integrating automation, Baumol effects, and idea production with clear links to AI and growth. Rigorous, influential, and careful about assumptions and limits. Empirical support is illustrative rather than definitive; no replication materials. Overall, among the stronger recent contributions in macro-AI.

Claims are clearly scoped and supported by formal models (Zeira-style, CES, Schumpeter) and transparent simulations. Evidence is primarily theoretical with selective sectoral/descriptive facts; characterization of uncertainty and alternative cases is careful. Limited direct empirical testing or calibration.

Sound macro-theoretic modeling; assumptions explicit (e.g., ρ<0, exogenous automation). Explores robustness via alternative elasticities, regime switching, and idea-production channels. No structural estimation; automation path largely exogenous; simulations not fully reproducible. Mathematical arguments are credible and internally consistent.

Sharp conceptual contributions: links Baumol’s cost disease to automation, clarifies conditions for balanced growth vs. singularities, highlights idea-production automation, and firm-level channels. Has shaped subsequent research agendas and empirical tests. High marginal value for future impactful work.

Exceptional clarity: questions posed upfront, assumptions explicit, derivations transparent, and alternative cases discussed. Figures align with arguments; caveats and limits acknowledged. Narrative integrates theory, intuition, and implications coherently.

NBER working paper with equations and figures but no shared code or replication package. Data sources cited (KLEMS, IFR) but scripts not provided. Model details sufficient for theoreticians, yet empirical/simulation reproducibility is limited.

Highly relevant to global priorities: growth trajectories, automation impacts, inequality, market structure, and innovation policy. Offers mechanisms and qualitative guidance; limited quantified policy estimates or cost-benefit outputs reduce immediate practitioner usability.

High-quality saturation RCT across 133 villages with rich, high-frequency labor, employer, and price data. Credible identification of GE spillovers and wage effects. Some reliance on retrospective employer measures and a few weak first-stage IVs in HF data; limited multiple-testing adjustments; unclear data/code release dampens score slightly.

Main claims (strategic complementarities in migration, higher village wages and work hours, small food price changes, employer profit squeeze) are well-supported via ITT/IV and multiple datasets. Caveats: employer profit estimates partly retrospective with instability; some HF IVs weak; multiple outcomes with no MHT correction.

Strong design: randomized saturation of offers, pre-registration, clustered inference, multiple data sources, HF surveys, village-level first stages for GE analysis. Assumptions (closed village labor markets) checked. Weaknesses: some weak IV in subsamples, retrospective recall for employers, limited formal robustness on multiple hypothesis testing.

Provides rare experimental evidence on general equilibrium effects of internal seasonal migration subsidies. Quantifies wage, labor supply, price, and employer impacts; informs debates on mobility restrictions vs. rural programs. External validity and later scale-up performance uncertain but contribution remains substantial.

Clear statement of questions, simple organizing model, and consistent empirical narrative. Tables link first-stage migration shifts to wages, hours, prices, and profits. Limitations acknowledged. A few complex sections (employer finances, timing selection) but overall transparent and coherent.

Trial pre-registered (AEA registry). Implementation and measurement well-documented. However, no clear public data/code repository is linked; replication would be heavy. Limited sharing of analysis scripts or materials visible in the WP.

Highly relevant to policy on seasonal poverty, internal migration, and labor markets in LMICs. Quantifies direct and spillover effects, informing design/scale-up and trade-offs (laborers vs. employers). Applicability beyond Bangladesh likely, though context dependence remains.

Large, well-executed nationwide Twitter RCT with clever identification of endorsement vs reach. Strong online effects; offline impacts are suggestive and cautiously framed. Pre-registration and thoughtful robustness checks. Main limitations: external validity beyond Indonesia/Twitter 2015–16, reliance on likes/retweets and self-reported survey outcomes, limited power for behavioral change. Policy relevance is high; conclusions are measured.

Core questions clearly stated. Causal claims on endorsement and sourcing supported by randomized authorship/sourcing and F1/F2 design; forced retweets address selection. RI p-values and clustering used; content controls applied. Offline results are presented as ‘suggestive’ with appropriate caveats. Multiple-testing adjustments are limited, and reliance on p-values over intervals reduces transparency somewhat.

Strong design: randomized tweet timing/content/authorship/sourcing; decomposition of reach vs endorsement via F2 “blinding”; forced F1 retweets; exposure–response analysis. Appropriate Poisson models, FE, clustering, and tests for retweet-count display confound. Limitations: survey sample via promoted ads, self-reports, partial MT correction, platform-specific context. Pre-registered and IRB-approved.

Provides rare causal evidence on influencer endorsement effects at national scale; overturns common assumptions (sources reduce diffusion), and informs complex contagion vs simple contagion. Offers actionable guidance for public-health messaging. Generalizability across platforms, topics, and eras is uncertain, and hard outcomes are limited, but the contribution meaningfully advances both theory and practice.

Clear articulation of goals, design schematics, and logic. Assumptions and threats to identification are explicit; appendixed model connects theory to findings. Tables/figures are interpretable; conclusions match evidence and are cautious. Minor weaknesses: heavy econometric focus with few intuitive uncertainty summaries; multiplicity discussion could be deeper.

AEA registry and IRB approvals are provided; design is well-documented. However, Twitter Firehose data likely cannot be shared; no clear public replication package/code is indicated. Survey data availability is unclear. Platform changes hinder exact reproduction. Overall: moderate transparency, constrained by data rights.

Highly relevant to vaccination promotion and broader public-health communication, especially in LMIC contexts. Offers practical, testable design rules (use influential endorsements, be cautious with sourcing, optimize exposures). Lacks cost-effectiveness and verified health outcomes, but insights are readily applicable for campaign design and policy.

High-impact theory plus careful empirics. Provides a portable sufficient-statistics framework tying nudges, pass-through, and variance/targeting to welfare; implements it in two preregistered RCTs. Transparent about limits (proxy-based bias in drinks, lab-like choices, potential demand effects). Replication files available. Likely to shape future work and policy debates on labels vs taxes.

Core claims (average effects can mislead; variance/targeting and pass-through matter) are theoretically derived and empirically illustrated. They estimate ATEs, Var(τ), Cov(τ, bias/externalities), and conduct sensitivity to ρ and μ. Limits: drinks bias relies on proxies; some covariance estimates are noisy; external validity is limited. Claims are carefully scoped and caveated.

Rigorous theory (Weyl–Fabinger conduct, endogenous prices) and implementable sufficient statistics. Empirics use randomized labels, adaptive incentivized MPLs, mixed-effects to identify heterogeneity. Registration done; no PAP due to structural modeling. Assumptions (normality, independence of measurement error, pass-through from literature) are reasonable but nontrivial. Robustness and appendices are strong.

Reorients welfare evaluation of nudges toward heterogeneity/targeting and interaction with taxes and pass-through; supplies estimable formulas and a template for measurement. Bridges behavioral public finance and applied nudge evaluation. Likely to influence policy design (labels with taxes) and future empirical practice.

Clear statement of goals, assumptions, and derivations; intuitive examples; diagrams; thorough appendices. Results tied back to literature (libertarian/asymmetric paternalism). Minor drawbacks: heavy notation and length may challenge some readers.

Trials registered (AEARCTR, ClinicalTrials.gov); IRB approvals; replication files posted; detailed appendices and sensitivity analyses. Some data come from panels/shipping logistics limiting full openness; no pre-analysis plan. Still above-average transparency and reproducibility.

High relevance to global priorities: climate/energy (fuel economy) and public health (SSBs). Offers actionable guidance on when nudges help or hurt, especially alongside taxes. Insights generalize to other markets with externalities and market power.

Large, carefully assembled multi-source dataset; clear conceptual framework; strong and consistent results across outcomes; inventive IV using subcommittee composition. Credible robustness and heterogeneity analyses. Remaining concerns about exclusion restrictions, exposure-share endogeneity, and measurement noise temper the top rating.

Main questions and claims are explicit. Evidence triangulates patents, publications, scientist employment, R&D spend, and firm value, with coherent signs and magnitudes. Authors are generally cautious in interpretation. Causal claims rest on IV assumptions that, while argued for and stress‑tested, are not airtight.

Shift–share IVs built from predicted agency R&D budgets via political composition, plus rich fixed effects and alternative instruments. Strong first stages and many robustness checks. Risks remain: exclusion restriction, correlated exposure shares, text-similarity weighting choices, and reliance on proprietary bibliometrics.

Important advance separating ‘publications, patents, people’ channels with firm-level relevance measures. Policy-relevant insight that human capital boosts, while public inventions can crowd out, incumbent R&D; life-science exception documented. Likely to shape debates on university tech transfer and science policy.

Goals, constructs, and assumptions are clearly laid out; theory maps to empirics. Tables and appendices are thorough; heterogeneity and robustness are well explained. Limitations discussed, though some threats could be more explicitly stress-tested.

Helpful methodological detail and some referenced datasets (e.g., DISCERN/Zenodo). However, substantial reliance on proprietary sources (Dimensions, ProQuest, AMWS) limits full reproducibility; unclear public code release; complex linkages may be hard to replicate independently.

Findings inform science/innovation policy, university tech transfer, and corporate R&D strategy—relevant to productivity and growth. Strongest applicability for U.S. context; indirect for practitioners outside policy/innovation ecosystems; limited direct cost–benefit quantification.

Compelling causal study of Colombia’s PEP using innovative RVI-fuzzy RD with large admin linkage; strong first stage, balance/placebo checks, dynamics and panel corroboration. Clear policy relevance and methodological contribution. Main caveats: model-dependent mapping from rain to queue order; assumptions on within-week exchangeability; outcome limited to formal firm registrations; replication limited by data access.

Main claims (legal status substantially boosts entrepreneurship; effect grows over time; larger than relocation) are well-stated and supported via IV, placebo, heterogeneity, and panel DiD. LATE interpretation is explicit. Evidence that effects reflect new creation vs formalization is suggestive (timing) but not definitive. Mechanisms discussed plausibly.

Novel running-variable instrument via rainfall permutations embedded in fuzzy RD/2SLS; controls for expected instrument; strong first-stage; manipulation and balance tests; complementary panel. Risks: reliance on fitted mapping from precipitation to census order, monotonicity, local randomization within week×city. Robustness variants help, but residual model dependence remains.

First rigorous micro-evidence on legalization’s impact on entrepreneurship among undocumented migrants in a LMIC; quantifies sizable effects reaching parity with natives; separates relocation vs rights; provides methodological advance generalizable to other threshold settings. High value for migration, development, and entrepreneurship policy.

Objectives, context, and assumptions are clearly laid out; formal framework aids transparency; figures/tables are informative; stacked RD diagnostics and dynamic plots persuasive. Some sections are complex; sensitivity to instrument construction could be summarized more accessibly; otherwise coherent and consistent.

Administrative RAMV–RUES data likely restricted; weather data proprietary; paper includes detailed appendices and specs but no clear public replication package noted. Methods are reproducible in principle; actual reanalysis requires data agreements. Useful building blocks (design, equations) provided.

Directly relevant to global migration policy and regularization programs; offers actionable magnitudes and timing; speaks to entrepreneurship, job creation, and integration in LMICs. Findings generalize conceptually to other amnesties; high usefulness for practitioners and policymakers.

Introduces TVA with theory, simulations, and a large policy-scale RCT; provides actionable best-policy estimates with winner’s-curse correction. Assumptions (beta-min, homoskedastic errors, pointwise asymptotics) and moderate openness temper a perfect score.

Claims on TVA performance and policy effects are supported by formal results, extensive simulations, a large cross-randomized RCT, administrative data validation, robustness and bootstraps. Some dependence on tuning (λ), administrative data coverage, and partial sensitivity remain.

Sound reparameterization, Puffer-transformed LASSO for support, post-selection OLS, and Andrews–Kitagawa–McCloskey correction. Assumptions explicit; proofs and simulations thorough. Caveats: homoskedasticity in Puffer theory, beta-min/local-alternative constraints, non-uniform asymptotics.

Fills a key gap for large factorial policy selection, blending selection, estimation, and winner’s-curse adjustment. Likely to shape experimental design/analysis and practical policy choice beyond immunization.

Goals and constructs are clear; Hasse diagrams and stepwise algorithm help; limitations are stated. Technical density may challenge some applied readers, but reasoning is generally transparent and coherent.

Design details and appendices are rich; validation documented. However, explicit public code/data repositories are not evident here. Reproducibility would improve with released code and (de-identified or synthetic) data.
Addresses child immunization uptake at scale with government partnership; cost-effectiveness focus; TVA applicable to many multi-arm policy settings, enhancing decision-making under constraints.

Introduces a principled TVA procedure and applies it to a very large, policy-relevant RCT. Strong identification, careful post-selection inference (winner’s curse), extensive simulations, and actionable results. Assumptions (sparsity/beta-min, K<n, homoskedasticity in theory) and some opacity on full replication resources temper a top score.

Main questions and claims are explicit; evidence includes a large factorial RCT, validated admin data, rich robustness and simulations, and coherent adjustments. Some reliance on strong assumptions and limited detail on pre-specification/λ choice may modestly weaken characterization of uncertainty.

Innovative combination of marginal-effects reparameterization, Puffer-preconditioned LASSO, post-selection OLS, and winner’s-curse correction. Assumptions are stated and justified; proofs and simulations support validity. Limitations: beta-min/local alternatives, homoskedasticity in theory, and practical sensitivity to tuning.

TVA is a useful methodological advance for selecting among many treatment bundles; contributes to design/analysis of factorial trials with interactions. Applied findings (synergies among hubs, incentives, SMS; cost-effectiveness) are informative for practice and future research.

Clear structure, explicit assumptions, helpful Hasse diagrams, algorithms, and detailed appendices. Arguments are logically consistent and cautious about scope. Dense proofs and length may challenge accessibility for some readers.

Open working paper and extensive appendices, simulations described well. However, no clear public replication package/code and underlying administrative data likely not shareable; preregistration details unclear.

Directly targets childhood immunization in LMICs with scalable, cost-aware policy guidance. Method generalizes to other policy bundle settings; results are highly actionable for governments and implementers focused on global health impact.

Large multi-community RCT with strong short-run impacts on mental/physical health, socioemotional skills, cognition, and economic expectations. Careful randomization, RI-based inference, and heterogeneity via LASSO. Limitations: 2–3 month horizon, heavy reliance on self-reports, unclear pre-registration, potential demand effects, and uncertain persistence/generalizability.

Core claims are generally supported: robust improvements and suggestive evidence for vulnerability and bandwidth channels. Heterogeneity patterns align with theory. However, bandwidth evidence on cognition is modest, economic outcomes are proximate, and the ‘core human capital strategy’ framing extrapolates beyond measured horizons and objective outcomes.

Well-powered, multi-stage randomization with re-randomization for balance, RI, and holdout LASSO. Addresses spillovers; manualized delivery; indices pre-standardized. Weaknesses: short follow-up; self-reports; no clear PAP or multiple-testing adjustments beyond RI; no blinding; limited objective outcomes; potential demand effects.

Shows general-population, lay-delivered CBT can improve multiple human-capital dimensions; introduces vulnerability risk-scoring heterogeneity; links therapy to bandwidth. Contrasts with prior nulls, informing design intensity/timeframes. High policy salience. Key gaps: durability, scaling fidelity, and cost-effectiveness over longer horizons.

Clear motivation and theory (vulnerability, scarcity/bandwidth), transparent specifications, thorough tables, and structured ethics appendix. Reasoning largely consistent with evidence; mechanisms carefully caveated. Some extrapolations ambitious; technical details heavy but generally well explained.

CBT manual and ethics appendix available; heterogeneity procedure described. However, no evident public replication package or data/code in WP; pre-registration unspecified; limited materials for turnkey reproduction reduce replicability.

Mental health in LMICs is a major priority; group CBT by lay counselors is scalable and integrable (e.g., Ghana NSS). Evidence of multi-domain gains with potential for broad human-capital impacts. Uncertainty about long-run persistence and cost-effectiveness tempers certainty but relevance is high.

Strong synthesis of evolutionary theory and empirics. Clear predictions, multiple validations (DRC + WVS), and careful framing (associations, not causality). Limitations: measurement via perceptions, residual endogeneity, and no sharp identification. Nonetheless, breadth, coherence, and robustness checks justify a high overall rating.

Core claims are explicit and matched to testable predictions. Evidence triangulates vignette validation, local surveys, and global WVS. Authors generally avoid causal overreach. Remaining concerns: reliance on perceived zero-sumness as proxy for α, potential reverse causality, and cultural measurement equivalence across countries.

Evolutionary model is well-specified with proofs and robustness. Empirics use FE, large samples, validation (employment, rainfall, growth), and within-α stratification. However, identification is correlational; potential omitted variables and response biases remain. Limited discussion of multiple-testing control and measurement invariance across cultures.

Introduces ‘demotivating beliefs’ in an evolutionary framework, aligning anthropology with economics. Novel prediction of hump-shaped welfare–belief relation within environments; connects to growth via learning-by-doing. Empirical patterns are broad and policy-relevant, likely to stimulate further causal and intervention research.

Concepts and assumptions are defined clearly; math derivations and comparative statics are transparent. Empirical sections are logically structured with ample robustness and appendices. Figures and validations support the narrative. Minor complexity may challenge non-specialists, but overall communication is excellent.

WVS data are public; appendices are detailed. However, no clear release of DRC microdata/code or preregistration; reproducibility may be partial. Sharing analysis scripts and survey microdata (de-identified) would substantially improve replicability.

High relevance to development practice and policy: links perceived zero-sumness to beliefs, welfare, and well-being across contexts. Offers guidance for interventions that reduce zero-sum perceptions/competition externalities. Less immediately actionable for cost-effectiveness, but valuable for prioritizing socio-cultural levers.

Well-reasoned, practice-oriented framework for discounting RCT evidence in CEAs. Anchors guidance in replication/meta-science literature, separates internal vs external validity, offers actionable steps and a worked example. Biggest limitations: largely heuristic synthesis without new empirical validation; external validity guidance remains coarse; no implemented calculator or replication package. Still above-average usefulness for applied evaluators.

Key claims (Type M prevalent; Type S rare; external validity highly variable) are supported by credible sources (Gelman & Carlin, Vivalt, Camerer, OSC, Button, Ioannidis). Caveats are explicit. Some numerical rules-of-thumb (e.g., 50–60% Type M discount; 99% generalization spread) risk overgeneralization; RoBMA preprint cited cautiously.

Method is structured expert synthesis with literature-based heuristics and suggested Bayesian tools (retrodesign). Sound reasoning on power/publication bias; clear checklists. Limited original analysis; no formal uncertainty propagation across steps; potential double-count risks (e.g., Hawthorne across internal/external) noted but not fully formalized. Robustness depends on user implementation.

Adds practical value by operationalizing replication and generalizability discounts for CEAs, likely improving consistency across evaluations. Advances practice more than theory. Particularly useful for early-stage or sparse-evidence interventions; less novel for well-studied domains.

Clear structure, definitions, and reasoning; good separation of internal vs external validity; step-by-step guidance and example. Transparent about uncertainties and limitations. Minor redundancies and reliance on figures external to the text; no formal decision tree or tool provided.

Extensive referencing and links; encourages use of open tools (retrodesign). However, no shared code, datasets, or templates; no preregistration; no packaged calculator or replication materials. Internal consistency reasonable but not auditable via artifacts.

Highly relevant to global health/development CEAs and charity recommendations; directly informs discounting of RCTs and quasi-experiments for policy/practice. Offers quantifiable adjustments and practitioner-focused guidance. General policymakers may need domain tailoring, but core insights travel well.

Compelling long-run follow-up of two psychotherapy RCTs in India. Strong, policy-relevant mental-health impacts (HAP) at 5 years, rigorous behavioral outcomes, careful analysis (DML, FDR), and clear nulls on economic outcomes. Communication and framing are excellent. Limitations: 24% attrition (balanced), limited power for THPP/heterogeneity, some PAP deviations, partial reliance on self-reports, and external validity constraints.

Main claims—persistent depression reduction (HAP), changes in belief-updating/overconfidence, no long-run economic gains—are well-supported by ITT estimates, PHQ-9 thresholds, incentivized tasks, and robustness checks with FDR. Expert-forecast benchmarking strengthens interpretation. Caveats: effects concentrated in HAP; belief-updating inference relies on task comprehension/model; mediation is exploratory; preference indices partly driven by self-assessments.

Sound RCT foundations with 4–5y tracking (76%), balanced attrition, DML controls, FDR within families, and transparent PAP deviations. Belief-updating modeled via logit-Bayes with robustness to exclusion rules. Assumptions reasonable. Weaknesses: limited power in THPP, many outcomes with partial multiplicity control, some unplanned modules, external validity constraints.

Provides rare long-run evidence on non-specialist psychotherapy’s persistence and cost-effectiveness; integrates behavioral-economics measures of confidence updating in LMICs; challenges depressive realism via causal evidence; documents important nulls on economic outcomes. High value for global mental health and development economics.

Clear questions, precise constructs, logical flow, and transparent reasoning. Detailed appendices, figures, and robustness. Deviations from PAP are disclosed; multiple-testing corrections explained. Minor scope to streamline generalizability discussion and emphasize limits of self-reported preference measures.

IRB approval, AEA pre-registration (AEARCTR-0003823), extensive appendices, and expert-forecast pre-specification. However, public availability of data/code is unclear; some outcomes were added post-PAP; not all materials appear archived for replication.

High relevance to global priorities: scalable, low-cost psychotherapy in LMICs; ~9 months of depression averted over 5 years at ~$7/month; insights on demand formation and belief updating; policy-relevant nulls for economic outcomes. Applicability broad but sample largely female in Goa with labor-market constraints.

Compelling, clear argument that citation-centric incentives depress exploration, with plausible mechanism and actionable proposals (novelty/edge metrics). Draws on credible literature and authors’ prior work. However, causal evidence is limited, and the paper adds little new empirical analysis or open materials. Strong but not elite.

Main claims are explicit and supported by case studies (PCR, CRISPR), cited empirical literature (e.g., HHMI natural experiment), and a simple model. Evidence is largely suggestive; the causal link from citation incentives to stagnation is not rigorously identified, and alternative explanations receive limited testing.

Relies on a stylized lifecycle model and narrative review. The novelty-versus-impact illustration leans on prior text-mining work without methodological detail, robustness checks, or shared code. Assumptions (e.g., mapping terms to ideas) are plausible but not validated here.

Reframes incentive design by proposing to measure and reward novelty alongside impact; delineates roles for search engines and funders. Provides a unifying conceptual framework with policy relevance. Limited by absence of implementation trials or quantitative policy evaluation in this paper.

Lucid, well-structured narrative; figures effectively convey the lifecycle concept. Assumptions and steps are mostly explicit. Some overreach when moving from correlational evidence to macro-stagnation conclusions, but overall reasoning is coherent and persuasive.

No shared data or code; empirical illustration not reproducible from this paper. Sources are clearly cited, but tools/resources are not provided. Relies on prior datasets and proprietary platforms; limited transparency hinders replication.

Highly pertinent to global research policy and innovation portfolios; recommendations could shift incentives toward higher-risk exploration across fields and countries. Practicality is decent but lacks detailed implementation playbooks and quantified impact/cost analyses.

Addresses an important, policy-relevant question with a novel framing. Communication is transparent about severe limitations. However, contingent valuation with highly hypothetical scenarios, extreme skew/outliers, small effective samples, and ad hoc exclusions make quantitative estimates fragile. Good for qualitative insight and agenda-setting, weak for calibration.

Claims that many view farm-animal lives as not worth living and that chicken welfare costs dominate are partly supported by medians and nonparametrics. However, evidence hinges on fragile CV responses, sensitivity to exclusion/outlier rules, low power, and an unvalidated representative-agent mapping. Authors appropriately flag uncertainty; quantitative claims remain tentative.

Uses online panel, randomized ordering, certainty scales, and nonparametric tests. Yet scenario is extremely hypothetical/transformative; high inconsistency and attrition; low power; arbitrary outlier handling; large WTA–WTP gaps; limited robustness to analytic choices; no pre-registration or multiple-testing corrections. Suitable for exploratory work, not precise estimation.

Contributes by explicitly monetizing animal-welfare externalities and linking them to optimal meat taxation and climate externalities. Highlights misalignment between consumer concern and welfare impact. Though estimates are too fragile for policy calibration, the conceptual framework and qualitative insights advance discussion and future research directions.

Clear statement of goals; solid theoretical setup; assumptions mostly explicit; tables and sensitivity analyses aid transparency. Limitations are candidly discussed. Some conceptual leaps (representative-agent WTP equating to welfare costs; critical-level interpretations) and complexity may confuse; nonetheless generally coherent and careful.

Procedures and key survey items are described, but no public data, code, or pre-registration are provided. Results are highly sensitive to analytic choices, increasing the need for open materials. Replicability is therefore limited despite reasonable methodological description.

Highly relevant to global priorities and animal welfare policy, with implications for meat taxation and consumer guidance (e.g., chicken). External validity beyond Belgium and quantitative reliability limit immediate decision-use, but the work is useful for agenda-setting and highlighting multi-externality interactions.

Nationwide randomized field experiment with strong identification, mechanism and spillover tests, and sizable, policy-relevant effects. Robust analyses and clear results. Minor weaknesses: partial general-equilibrium design (95% vs 70% only), external validity beyond China, and modest openness of data/code.

Main claims align directly with randomized assignments (public vs private appeals), visibility manipulation, and cross-randomized intensity. Strong fixed-effects designs, appropriate clustering, event studies, and falsification tests (manipulation checks). Some mechanism evidence (career incentives) is partly correlational.

Well-powered firm-level RCT; careful verification of violations; province-by-day FEs; two-way clustering; appeal-level randomization for visibility; spillover assessment via intensity cross-randomization. Concerns: measurement noise in verification, limited power for ambient outcomes, no zero-intensity cities, and limited multiple-testing adjustments.

Provides first large-scale experimental evidence that social-media public appeals shift regulator behavior and reduce emissions, with rare GE evidence. Integrates citizen–state–firm dynamics. High impact for environmental governance; external portability uncertain but informative.

Objectives, design, and theory of change are clear; figures/tables match arguments; limitations discussed. Some auxiliary analyses are extensive and placed in appendices; narrative could be streamlined, but reasoning remains transparent and consistent.

Pre-registered (AEARCTR-0005601) with data appendix and detailed protocols. However, core administrative datasets are restricted; no public code repository is evident; full replication requires privileged access.

Addresses major global burden (pollution) with scalable, low-cost citizen-participation lever; provides quantitative effects and cost-benefit sketch. Institutional dependence on China’s CEMS/social media limits direct transfer, but lessons are valuable for LMIC regulators and civic-tech practitioners.

Ambitious, careful program (9 experiments; N≈5,776) mapping population-ethics intuitions. Strong design, clear findings (negativity asymmetry; average vs total tradeoffs), extensive limitations discussion, open materials. Main caveats: online US samples, vignette/hypothetical measures, construct validity of “happiness scales,” some non-preregistered studies.

Core questions explicit; results replicated across multiple manipulations and designs. Pre-registered in several studies; comprehension/attention checks; effect sizes and uncertainty reported; alternative explanations discussed. Some studies (2a–2b) not preregistered; reliance on hypothetical judgments limits external validity.

Appropriate sampling (MTurk/Prolific), a priori power, preregistrations, attention/comprehension checks, and reasonable analyses (t-tests/ANOVAs; some multiple-comparison controls). Robustness via varied framings. Limitations: convenience samples, hypothetical scenarios, partial multiple-testing control, some comprehension failures, and two unpreregistered studies.

Among the first systematic psychological investigations of population-ethics intuitions; clarifies average vs total and asymmetry patterns and effects of reflection. Bridges moral psychology and philosophy; informs debates in longtermism. Not directly prescriptive; generalizability and ecological validity constrain impact.

Well-structured program with clear research questions, definitions, and careful reasoning. Figures/tables aid comprehension; limitations candidly treated. Some complexity and length may burden readers; numeric “happiness scale” remains conceptually demanding.

Data, code, and materials publicly available (OSF); multiple preregistrations; ethics approvals; reporting of measures/manipulations/exclusions. Not all studies preregistered, but overall transparency is excellent.

Findings inform communication and policy framing for longtermism, extinction risk, and population policy by illuminating public intuitions. Indirect practical utility; no intervention estimates; cultural scope uncertain beyond US online samples.

Rigorous head-to-head of epidemiological accounting vs reduced-form designs on measles. Strong validation of the SIR-based measure for outbreaks; reduced-form estimates robust for long-run outcomes and mortality. Sensitivity analyses are informative. Limitations: identifying assumptions (parallel trends, unmeasured confounding tied to pre-vaccine mortality), uniform vaccination rates, age-risk simplifications, and unclear replication materials.

Main claims are clear: epidemiological model predicts outbreaks; reduced-form better captures long-run human capital/health impacts, implying severity matters more than infection shares. Evidence aligns: robustness with cohort FEs only for reduced-form; mortality patterns corroborate. Some risk of over-generalizing beyond measles/US context is acknowledged but not deeply probed.

Thoughtful SIR-based accounting (reporting-rate estimation; susceptibles dynamics) with validations and sensitivity checks. Reduced-form is standard and well-implemented (state/cohort/age FEs; clustering). Key assumptions are strong: age-independent infection risk (baseline), national vaccination rollout, possible confounding in mortality proxy; limited formal pre-trend/placebo tests.

Clarifies when epidemiological accounting helps (short-run outbreaks) vs reduced-form (long-run human capital), guiding proxy choice in vaccine impact research. Integrates epi-econ approaches and informs VoV/GP research. Incremental rather than transformative; focused on one disease/country but with clear implications.

Goals and contrasts are explicit; models and assumptions are described transparently with equations. Figures are clear and tie to narrative; results consistently compared across specifications. Limitations are discussed; reasoning is largely tight with few leaps.

Uses public data (Tycho, Vital Statistics, IPUMS) and cites sources clearly. However, no explicit replication package, code, or preregistration is evident from the text. Sensitivity analyses are reported but full reproducibility is uncertain.

Directly relevant to vaccination policy and valuing vaccine benefits; emphasizes larger gains in high-mortality settings—key for global priorities. Results mainly US/measles-specific; extrapolation to other pathogens contexts is reasoned but limited.

Rigorous, policy-relevant modeling of science’s social returns under biotech risk. Clear structure, careful caveats, and extensive sensitivity analysis. Some conclusions hinge on strong, contestable assumptions (epistemic-regime discounting, diffusion lags, mapping XPT outputs to annual mortality). Still, the work is thoughtful, transparent, and decision-informative.

Main claims (ROI 60x–330x; break-even d≈0.13–0.15% without extinction; extinction hinges on long-run value) are stated clearly and supported by transparent models plus XPT calibration. Evidence characterization is careful with uncertainties noted. Reliance on forecasts and parameter choices limits external validation.

Stylized utility/growth framework with two health models, explicit lags, and derivation of annualized peril rates from XPT. Good sensitivity and bounding cases. Key mappings involve strong assumptions; no formal probabilistic model or empirical validation; some feedbacks and alternative priors could be explored.

Integrates metascience economics with biosecurity risk into a quantitative, decision-focused framework; provides actionable thresholds and scenarios. Clarifies when accelerating science is net positive/negative and how extinction valuations pivot conclusions. Likely to shape funder and policy discussions.

Exceptionally clear exposition, transparent assumptions, stepwise derivations, and decompositions (peril/income/health). Strong executive summary and appendices. Minor complexity remains in the XPT-to-d mapping, but reasoning is traceable.

Detailed equations, parameter justifications, and technical appendices. However, full replication materials (code/data) are not clearly provided; no preregistration. Reproduction would require re-implementation.

Directly targets global priorities: social ROI of science, biosecurity risks, and AI-era policy. Offers quantitative guidance for funders and policymakers with explicit break-evens and scenario analyses. Broad practical salience.

Rigorous, policy-relevant meta-analysis with careful bias adjustments and transparent limitations. Extends literature to learning scores, triangulates with quasi-experiments and Oster bounds, and offers clear simulations. Some reliance on re-expression, imputation, and observational studies with high heterogeneity temper confidence.

Core claims are clearly stated and appropriately caveated. Evidence from 47 studies, multiple bias adjustments, and supportive quasi-experimental findings are synthesized well. Characterization of non-experimental nature and confounding risks is forthright.

Solid search strategy; robust variance estimation; validated re-expression algorithm; PET-PEESE, trim-and-fill, p-uniform*, Copas; meta-regression with study-level moderators. Limits: very high I2, observational base, some imputation/transformations, sparse IV with BLL, and no preregistration noted.

Adds learning outcomes beyond IQ, quantifies contribution to cross-country learning gaps, and maps intervention classes to plausible gains—useful for prioritization. Consolidates disparate literatures for LMIC policy.

Clear goals, transparent assumptions, and coherent argumentation. Specification curves, forest plots, funnel plots, and sensitivity figures aid interpretation. Limitations and uncertainties are explicit.
Detailed methods and appendices facilitate understanding, but no evident preregistration and unclear public availability of extraction sheets/code/data limit full reproducibility.
Directly targets a widespread LMIC hazard with quantified education impacts and policy levers. Highly actionable for global health, education, and regulation agendas.

Ambitious cross-risk CE analysis with transparent assumptions and sensitivity work. However, heavy reliance on small, potentially biased expert elicitation and strong structural assumptions (independence of risks, mixed horizons, logarithmic returns) limit robustness. Useful but not definitive.

Main claim—resilient foods likely more cost-effective than AGI safety at the current margin—is supported within-model via Monte Carlo and sensitivity checks. Evidence rests on subjective priors, small-N survey (incl. affiliated respondents), and strong modeling choices; theory uncertainty is acknowledged but not fully propagated.

Framework (Monte Carlo/Latin hypercube, lognormal/beta priors) is reasonable and documented. Key weaknesses: small, potentially biased elicitation; independence between submodels; inconsistent time horizons; ad hoc marginal comparisons ($3B vs ~$100M); limited external validation. Sensitivity analysis helps but doesn’t span structural alternatives.

Pushes forward comparative cost-effectiveness across cause areas; elevates resilient foods with quantified arguments; identifies leverage points and urgency. Likely to inform portfolios and spur further research, though results depend on contestable inputs.

Goals, assumptions, and limitations are stated clearly; diagrams/tables help. Logical flow is generally sound, with explicit caveats. Some overinterpretation of within-model confidence and dense presentation of priors reduce clarity.

Guesstimate links and survey instrument provided; input tables detailed. Analytica model and raw survey data not fully open; no versioned code/data repository. Replication possible in part but not turnkey.

Directly targets high-priority global risks and actionable preparedness (10% and 100% shortfalls), with implications for funding strategy and timing. Highly pertinent to policymakers and philanthropists focused on existential and humanitarian outcomes.

Strong preregistered lab–field design; causal identification via MPL-induced randomization and IPW; consistent short-run effects and heterogeneity; transparent analyses and robustness checks. Limitations: student sample, COVID-reduced N vs preregistration, outcomes confined to canteens, short-lived effects, and unclear code/data availability. Still among the stronger recent papers in this area.

Claims (existence of avoiders, greater responsiveness of avoiders, and decay within ~2 weeks) are well supported by lab outcomes and linked field purchases, with placebos and robustness. Exploratory mediation handled cautiously. Some heterogeneity estimates in field are imprecise; outcome limited to canteens.

Innovative preference-respecting randomization (MPL WTP) with correct IPW identification of ATE/CATE. Balance checks, theoretical/empirical propensities, WLS robustness, placebos, and preanalysis mapping. Constraints: smaller N, student context, potential demand/VR narrative bundling, limited long-term measurement.

Adds rare field-based causal evidence on willful ignorance and actionable guidance (target avoiders; small incentives). Documents decay and modest cost-effectiveness. Valuable extension beyond lab studies, though limited to one domain and population; generalizability to other moral/health/risk domains remains to be shown.

Clear goals, definitions, and reasoning; mapping to preregistration; figures/tables support narrative; assumptions and limitations explicit; exploratory parts labeled. Minor complexity in moving-window presentation, but overall very well communicated.

Pre-registered (AEARCTR-0005015), IRB approval, detailed appendices, scene transcripts, and regulatory context. However, no explicit public code/data repository is cited; administrative data likely restricted. Reproducibility would improve with shared code and synthetic/anon data.

Directly relevant to animal welfare and design of information campaigns (also climate/health). Practical insight: near-zero info cost is insufficient; target avoiders with small incentives. External validity limited (German students, canteen purchases); effects fade quickly, tempering practical impact.

Well-framed application of public-goods theory to pharma pricing with transparent country-level calculations and simple regressions. Useful quantification (US ≈66–73% of global quasi-rents). Methods are serviceable but rely on strong assumptions (uniform MC, proxies from Turkey/CEA, quasi-rents→R&D) and limited identification. Communication is clear; open-science is weak.

Main claims—ROW contributes materially; GDP strongly predicts contributions; free-riding is partial—are supported by RAND price indices, two MC scenarios, and OLS results (Tables 4–5). Evidence is consistent but rests on debatable measurement choices and assumptions linking quasi-rents to R&D incentives; limited exploration of alternative mechanisms or drug-level heterogeneity.

Approach is transparent and reasonable for a first-cut: two MC estimates, simple conversion from prices to quasi-rents, log-OLS on GDP with robustness checks. Key weaknesses: crude MC proxies, uniform MC across countries, potential double-counting/distribution margins, endogeneity/tautology in GDP regressions, small n, no causal design, no micro-level validation.

Provides policy-relevant quantification of national contributions and challenges the ‘near-MC abroad’ narrative. Integrates alliance/public-goods theory with contemporary data, offering actionable order-of-magnitude estimates for burden-sharing debates. Incremental rather than transformative; lacks causal mapping from prices to innovation outputs.

Clear statement of questions, theoretical setup (Samuelson/Lindahl; Nash), and derivations. Empirical steps and sensitivity choices are explained; tables/figures aid comprehension. Some long expository sections and occasional conflation of quasi-rents with actual R&D financing persist, but overall argumentation is coherent and consistent.

Relies on public sources (RAND, PWT), but no shared code/data package, preregistration, or computational appendix to fully reproduce transformations and regressions. Replication is possible with effort but not facilitated. Limited reporting of exact drug baskets and robustness to alternative price adjustments.

Highly relevant to global priorities: financing biomedical innovation, international cost sharing, and policy design (e.g., negotiation, value-based pricing, trade-like agreements). Provides quantitative inputs for cross-country burden-sharing and R&D incentive discussions with direct implications for health outcomes and welfare.

Strong, timely contribution in climate/ESG finance: novel biodiversity news index, multiple firm/industry exposure measures, and pricing tests. Validation against events, cross-measure agreement, and comparisons to a large factor zoo are persuasive. Limits: US-centric data (NYT, 10-K), short time series, modest hedge correlations, some heuristic thresholds. Public release of exposure measures boosts impact.

Main claims (distinct biodiversity risk; measurable exposures; partial pricing) are clearly stated and appropriately qualified. Evidence triangulates news indices, 10-K text, survey, and fund holdings; event validation and cross-sectional correlations support claims. Pricing tests rely on correlations (not premia) and are framed as such. Potential survey selection bias and media/source limitations are acknowledged.

Reasonable, transparent approach: dictionary+filters with BERT sentiment; AR(1) innovations; portfolio construction; multiple-testing correction vs 207 characteristics; robustness via alternative weights. Assumptions: NYT as proxy for news, 10-K mentions/thresholds, few biodiversity ETFs (limited history), survey design. Mostly defensible, though external validity and measurement error risks remain. No causal estimates claimed.

First comprehensive, finance-oriented quantification of biodiversity risk and its pricing; creates reusable exposure datasets. Distinguishes biodiversity from climate in both time-series and cross-section. Likely to catalyze follow-on research and practical risk management. High marginal value despite unsurprising direction of results.

Clear motivation, definitions (physical vs transition risks), and transparent reasoning. Figures/tables effectively support the narrative. Limitations and scope are explicitly discussed (e.g., no risk premia inference). Minor arbitrariness (e.g., sentence thresholds) is explained.

Exposure measures publicly released (website). Survey instrument and many implementation details documented. Some inputs are proprietary (CRSP/Compustat/NYT) and code availability is not fully explicit, limiting full reproduction. Nonetheless, provides useful building blocks.

Biodiversity risk is globally salient; outputs inform regulators, investors, and firms. Practical industry exposure rankings and hedge constructs aid risk management. Generalizability is tempered by US-centric sources (NYT, 10-K) and limited non-US testing; little direct cost–benefit quantification.

Ambitious, well-executed welfare synthesis across 96 climate policies using a harmonized MVPF framework, new LBD sufficient-statistics result, extensive robustness, and clear contrasts with cost-per-ton. Some conclusions hinge on SCC/incidence and LBD assumptions, which are carefully probed.

Main claims (wind/solar > other subsidies; nudges context-dependent; fuel taxes/cap-and-trade low-MVPF raisers) are supported via consistent translations from causal estimates, harmonized externality valuations, and sensitivity analyses. Remaining uncertainties: incidence on US Treasury, AVERT marginal rates, cross-context elasticity transport, and LBD causality.

Careful MVPF construction (pass-through, markups, fiscal externalities, rebound) and formal LBD integration. Multiple SCC scenarios, with/without LBD, US-only benefits, publication-bias correction, non-marginal changes. Limitations: partial-equilibrium approximations, elasticity portability, potential sectoral GE effects.

Shifts policy evaluation from cost-per-ton to MVPF; provides actionable rankings and a reusable template. The LBD sufficient-statistics result is methodologically novel and broadly applicable. Rich comparisons (tax vs regulation; domestic vs international) directly inform prioritization.

Goals, assumptions, and steps are explicit; equations and decompositions are tight; figures/tables integrate well. Length and technical density may challenge some readers; a few choices (e.g., AVERT region aggregation) could be flagged earlier, but reasoning remains transparent.

Extensive appendices, parameter sources, bootstrap CIs, and stated public code availability; heavy use of public datasets/models (EPA, EIA). Minor risks: reproduction depends on multiple external tools and harmonizations; exact replication may require careful environment control.

Directly targets high-impact policy choices (subsidies, taxes, cap-and-trade) with quantified welfare metrics; includes international interventions and incidence considerations for US/global beneficiaries. Highly useful to policymakers, funders, and practitioners for near-term decisions.

Preregistered, large multi-arm RCT (n≈5,756) with rigorous design and analysis. Clear results: sizable cash effects; null PM+ at 1 year; careful spillover and demand-effect checks; low attrition; policy-relevant cost and frequency comparisons. Limitations: reliance on self-reports, 1-year horizon, context-specificity, and uncertain data/code availability.

Main claims are tightly linked to evidence. ANCOVA with baseline controls, clustering, and FDR across primary outcomes; precise estimates. Bayesian NPV frames nulls; experimenter-demand test implemented; heterogeneity and timing analyses; cautious interpretation of IPV and spillovers. Characterization of evidence is balanced and transparent.

Strong randomized design at village/household levels with four arms, spillovers, and weekly vs lump-sum. Preanalysis plan, power, low attrition, fidelity checks, appropriate clustering/ANCOVA, multiple-testing control. Sensible handling of DFS/M-Pesa overlap. Limits: self-reports, generalizability of CHW scaling, some cost-effectiveness assumptions, single endline horizon.

Rare head-to-head test of cash vs WHO PM+ in LMIC; challenges generalizability of brief psychotherapy; strengthens evidence on cash’s economic and psychological effects; informs delivery frequency. Decision-relevant for mental health vs cash prioritization. Less novel methodologically; external validity beyond setting and 1-year horizon remains open.

Clear motivation, questions, and pre-specified outcomes. Indices defined; tables/figures interpretable; assumptions and limitations discussed. Reasoning is transparent; robustness and alternative explanations considered. Minor density in appendices but overall narrative is coherent and consistent with results.

Pre-registered RCT (registry cited) with extensive online appendix, balance/attrition checks, and method details. However, public availability of data and analysis code is unclear; some operational data (M-Pesa) proprietary. Replication feasible but not turnkey without shared code/data.

Highly relevant to global poverty and mental health policy. Directly compares scalable interventions with costs and magnitudes; actionable for donors/governments in similar contexts. Offers guidance on targeting/intensity and cautions on psychotherapy without specific problem focus.

Compelling large-scale evidence of a pervasive, increasing pivot penalty across science and patents, supported by extensive robustness checks, within-person analyses, and quasi-experiments. Clear implications for science policy and organizational strategy. Main limitations: reliance on citations/journal placement as impact proxies, potential measurement error in pivot metric, and proprietary data impeding full replication.

Main claims (universal and rising pivot penalty; limited outsider advantage; COVID case; push/pull shocks) are supported by convergent evidence: binned plots, within-author FE, field-by-field regressions, patents and market value, preprint publication rates, DiD around retractions, and 2SLS. Causal language is cautious but not airtight; mechanisms are suggestive rather than proven.

Well-justified cosine pivot metric; multiple alternative encodings (journals vs fields; CPC hierarchy); extensive robustness on impact windows/measures; individual FE; DiD with matched controls; event studies; clustering; manual disambiguation checks. Concerns: measurement error in field/journal coding, remaining selection in natural experiments, reliance on binned scatters, limited multiple-testing adjustments, and proprietary datasets.

Establishes a strong new stylized fact quantifying adaptability costs and their growth, bridging science and technology with policy-relevant insights. Synthesizes mechanisms (reputation vs expertise) with novel empirical tests. COVID application adds salience. Likely to shape future research on specialization, funding design, and portfolio strategy.

Clear framing, definitions, and transparent reporting of assumptions; figures are informative; SI is thorough. Conclusions generally match evidence, with careful caveats. Some interpretive extensions (outsider advantage) could be more circumspect, but overall reasoning is coherent and easy to follow.

Methods are described in detail and several data sources are public (Retraction Watch via Crossref, PatentsView, SciSciNet, Kogan). However, core bibliometrics (Dimensions) are proprietary; no explicit code/data release is indicated, and some checks are ‘available on request’. Full computational reproducibility appears limited.

Highly relevant for funders, institutions, and policymakers managing responsiveness to crises (e.g., pandemics) and emerging domains (AI, climate). Provides actionable directional insights (pre-positioning, team strategies, portfolio diversification), though not cost-effectiveness estimates. Strong applicability across fields and stages.

High-quality RCT on a major environmental-health issue; clear, policy-relevant findings. Strong design (multiple arms), pre-analysis, and robust remote-sensing outcomes. Cost-effectiveness estimates are compelling. Main limitations: remote-sensing misclassification risk and training-label asymmetry, farmer-initiated monitoring for compliance, selected high-burning sample, and scalability/external-validity uncertainties.

Core claims (upfront PES improves compliance and reduces burning; standard PES largely inframarginal) are well-supported by multiple outcomes: monitored compliance, satellite-based measures, and CRM adoption. Sensitivity to classification thresholds is transparently shown. Cost-benefit framing is plausible but relies on VSL and attribution assumptions; authors note caveats.

Village-level stratified RCT, clustering, Lee bounds for attrition, pre-specification, and careful RS ML construction with threshold robustness. Concerns: negative (no-burn) labels from treatment group only, ~78–82% RS accuracy, farmer-initiated monitoring possibly inducing selection, screened high-burn sample, and some external-validity challenges.

Introduces and tests an important PES design feature (partial upfront unconditional payment) in a new application (residue burning), showing sizable effects and strong cost-effectiveness. Provides practical guidance for PES under trust/liquidity constraints and contributes a scalable RS measurement approach.

Clear articulation of motivation, design, and results; transparent discussion of monitoring, RS thresholds, and limitations. Tables/figures aid interpretation. Minor complexity around RS training/threshold choices, but overall reasoning is coherent and cautious.

Pre-registered (AEA RCT registry) with detailed methods and appendices. However, no clear public replication package; underlying commercial imagery may limit data sharing. RS model details referenced but full code/data availability is uncertain.

Addresses a large, neglected source of pollution with major health impacts; identifies a feasible, highly cost-effective intervention with clear policy design implications for India and similar contexts. Results inform broader PES and CCT design under weak enforcement and liquidity constraints.

Large preregistered US RCT with admin bank data; careful design and analysis; strong robustness and attrition bounds; informative null/negative findings versus optimistic priors; thoughtful mechanism tests and theory. Limits: differential response, bank data subsample, pandemic context, short horizon, sensitive data access.

Core claim—no positive survey effects despite higher spending—is strongly supported by ITT estimates, multiple-testing corrections, bank data, timing checks, and extensive attrition analyses (Lee/HM bounds, imputation). Mechanism evidence is suggestive (mediation) and appropriately caveated. Claims are accurately scoped to measured outcomes.

Power-optimized RCT, preregistered PAP, Anderson indices, BH/WY corrections, quasi-experimental timing, bank-data deduplication, numerous robustness checks, bounds and imputation. Assumptions and limitations discussed. Main weaknesses: reliance on self-reports for many outcomes, 43% bank-linking, one-off transfer amounts, HIC pandemic setting.

Recalibrates priors on UCTs in high‑income settings; integrates prediction study; clarifies objective vs subjective outcome divergence; proposes salience mechanism with model; informs ‘cash-plus’ and transfer size debates. External validity constrained (one-time, pandemic, short-term), but contribution is substantial.

Clear questions, thorough exposition, transparent assumptions, logical flow from results to mechanisms to model. Figures/tables support arguments; limitations candidly discussed. Dense but navigable appendices; minor complexity may challenge non-experts.

Preregistration and PAP public; instruments and extensive appendices provided; methods reproducible. Administrative/bank data likely restricted; code availability not fully clear. Strong transparency, slightly limited by data privacy constraints.

Highly relevant to cash transfer policy in HICs; tempers optimism, suggests larger or ‘cash‑plus’ designs, and attention to subjective well‑being. Lacks long-run and cost‑effectiveness estimates; pandemic timing limits generalizability across contexts.

High-quality, policy-relevant meta-analysis combining 18 RCTs with careful Bayesian and frequentist synthesis, extensive sensitivity checks, and clear cost-effectiveness modeling. Transparent about limitations (age/follow-up heterogeneity, limited mortality data, ICC assumptions). Strong open-science practices and clear communication. Minor concerns remain on generalizability and residual publication/selection biases.

Main claims are specific and supported by pooled estimates (OR≈0.72–0.75) with robustness across 64 sensitivity models and publication-bias checks. Evidence characterization is careful, acknowledging limited power for moderators and alternative priors. Clear distinction between historical mean and posterior predictive effects.

Appropriate random-effects meta-analysis; Bayesian hierarchical model with sensible priors; treatment of rare events; cluster adjustments; LOOCV; multiple sensitivity analyses including continuity corrections and contamination. Some choices (treating short follow-ups as U5 odds, ICC imputation, age-heterogeneity not modeled, limited moderator power) temper top-tier rigor.

Assembles new mortality data, shifts focus from diarrhea to all-cause child mortality, and links to credible cost-effectiveness estimates for scalable delivery models. Clarifies that water treatment likely averts substantial U5 deaths at very low cost, informing donors and governments. Provides directions for future heterogeneity and survival modeling.

Clear goals, transparent reasoning, explicit assumptions, and coherent presentation (PRISMA, forest plots, funnel plots). Results, limitations, and policy implications are well aligned. Minor density and cross-referencing could challenge some readers, but overall highly readable and logically consistent.

Pre-registered (AEARCTR-0005977), PRISMA assessed, code and data made public (GitHub), methods sufficiently detailed for replication. Some mortality data unavailable from legacy studies, but authors proactively contacted researchers. Provides tools/inputs enabling reanalysis and policy adaptation.

Directly targets a major global burden with scalable, low-cost interventions. Produces quantified DALY and net-benefit estimates ($27–$66/DALY), relevant to LMIC decision-makers and funders. Discusses delivery modalities (dispensers, inline chlorination, MCH), thresholds, and context-specific tradeoffs, enabling immediate policy use.

Rigorous causal design (SDID with seasonal controls), multiple robustness and placebo checks, and timely policy question. Clear evidence of positive spillovers; transparent discussion of limitations. Main weaknesses: substitutability assignment uncertainty, reliance on a single online platform, short post-period, and data/code not yet public. Strong but not definitive.

Main claim—trade bans increased volumes of non-banned substitutes—is supported across taxa with SDID estimates and CIs; sensitivity, single-species, monthly, and placebo analyses bolster credibility. However, external validity beyond the platform and substitutability misclassification temper strength; ecological impacts are inferred, not measured.

Appropriate use of SDID with two-step procedure, seasonal and fixed effects, removal of announcement quarter, extensive robustness/placebo checks. Assumptions (parallel trends, control construction, treated selection) are argued and partially validated. Short post-treatment window and platform coverage remain limitations.

Provides rare causal evidence of spillovers from wildlife trade bans using online market data; highlights policy-relevant unintended consequences and monitoring needs. Scope limited to Japan and a few taxa; does not quantify downstream ecological outcomes or enforcement responses.

Goals, setup, and findings are clear; figures align with narrative; assumptions and bias direction are discussed. Minor language/structure issues and limited main-text detail on NLP/species selection (mitigated by SI) slightly reduce clarity.

Methods are well-documented; SI provides details; GitHub release of data/code is promised upon publication. Current accessibility uncertain; dependence on third-party scraped data and NLP steps may complicate exact reproduction.

Wildlife trade bans and spillovers are globally salient for biodiversity policy (CITES, demand management). Findings generalize conceptually, though empirical focus is Japan/taxa-specific. Offers actionable insights for monitoring, enforcement, and demand-side interventions.

Ambitious, carefully executed multi-method study linking GDP to biodiversity using BioTIME, Bartik-style military shocks, CAA designations, and an upwind-pollution IV. Extensive robustness, heterogeneity, and dynamics. Clear policy relevance. Main limitations: state-level GDP vs site outcomes, BioTIME representativeness, and moderate instrument strength in the full sample.

Core claims (GDP reduces abundance, richness; stability effects; air pollution explains a sizable share; regulations mitigate) are stated clearly and consistently supported by OLS, 2SLS, and IV designs plus robustness. Limitations and scope are appropriately caveated (external validity, channel coverage).

Strong design: FE panels, Bartik instrument for GDP, LASSO-based upwind IV, CAA quasi-experiment, sectoral analyses, dynamics, spatial binning. Thoughtful sensitivity checks. Concerns: KP F≈7 in full-sample 2SLS; exclusion restrictions remain debatable; spatial scale mismatch; BioTIME selection and detectability issues.

Provides rare causal estimates of economy–biodiversity links across many taxa; quantifies air pollution’s contribution; shows regulatory co-benefits; integrates ecology datasets into econ frameworks. Offers reusable empirical templates and parameter estimates valuable for policy analysis and GP research.

Well-structured with clear definitions, stepwise logic, and extensive appendices/figures. Assumptions and identification strategies are discussed candidly. Some sections are dense; a condensed policy summary and clearer guidance on effect-size interpretation across metrics could improve readability.

Relies on public data (BioTIME, BEA, MERRA-2, EPA, WDPA) and documents processing and specifications thoroughly. However, replication packages/code availability are not clearly provided here; some constructed instruments and processing steps may be nontrivial without code.

High relevance to biodiversity conservation, environmental regulation, and macro–environment tradeoffs. Findings on CAA co-benefits and protected areas are actionable. US-focused sample limits direct transferability, but methods and insights generalize well to other contexts.

Comprehensive, decision-focused evaluation combining a large LMIC psychotherapy meta-analysis, charity-specific RCTs, and M&E with explicit validity adjustments, spillovers, and extensive sensitivity analyses. Main weaknesses: subjective evidence weighting, pseudo-synthetic controls for M&E, and thin spillover evidence. Nonetheless, claims are carefully bounded and robustness explored.

Main claims (WELLBY-based cost-effectiveness; 5–6x cash) are clearly stated, quantitatively supported, and caveated. Evidence spans 84 LMIC RCTs, charity RCTs, and very large M&E datasets. Uncertainties (dosage for FB; Baird et al. relevance; spillovers) are explicitly characterized with robustness checks. Some reliance on non-causal M&E limits inferential strength.

Approach is rigorous: multilevel meta-analysis with time-decay, multiple publication-bias corrections, range-restriction and dosage adjustments, and Monte Carlo propagation. Novel but reasonable handling of Iran effects and extreme follow-ups, with sensitivities. Weighting across evidence sources mixes Bayesian and structured judgment; defensible though subjective.

Advances WELLBY cost-effectiveness for mental health in LMICs; integrates spillovers; proposes a transparent framework to combine heterogeneous evidence; provides donor-relevant estimates and extensive appendices. Offers replicable procedures others can adapt. Less strong on definitive spillover magnitudes and fully formalized weighting, but overall high contribution.

Goals, assumptions, and analytical flow are explicit; figures and tables aid understanding. Reasoning is transparent with clear justifications for nonstandard choices and thorough sensitivity analyses. Length/complexity is high, but key messages remain clear and consistent with presented evidence.

Systematic review with protocol cited; double data checks; RoB assessments; external appendix and summary spreadsheet; methods detailed and implemented in R. However, full code/data availability is unclear and charity M&E microdata are private; some reproducibility constraints remain.

Directly targets neglected mental health in SSA with scalable charities; produces actionable, comparable cost-effectiveness vs cash transfers; informs donors and policymakers. Framework generalizes to other interventions and settings; strong practical relevance to global priorities.

Large, policy-relevant RCT with careful design, multiple follow-ups, admin linkage, attrition reweighting and bounds, and MTE to interpret selection. Clear first-stage, sizable effects, nuanced SWB findings. Some limits: attrition imbalance, partial external validity (two firms, construction), and linear MTE assumption.

Main claims (earnings gains, intermediary costs, SWB declines, heterogeneity) are tightly linked to randomized offers, IV estimates, admin imputation, and bounding. Expectations vs realizations bolster credibility. Remaining concerns: attrition sensitivity for SWB, self-reported outcomes, and some specification choices.

Well-executed RCT with site-day FE, clustered SEs, IV for treatment-on-treated, attrition weights, Manski bounds, admin data calibration, and linear MTE extrapolation. Assumptions: monotonicity, linear MTE, limited spillovers. Some outcomes are subjective; external validity mainly construction, UAE.

Rare experimental evidence on Gulf guest workers; quantifies intermediary fees, SWB costs, and heterogeneity informing the policy-efficiency debate. Integrates reservation wages and MTE. Substantially advances understanding of pecuniary vs non-pecuniary migration trade-offs.

Clear framing, transparent reporting, coherent tables/figures, and careful interpretation (ITT, IV, bounds). Mechanisms plausibly argued (pain/effort/heat). Some density of presentation and heavy appendices may challenge non-specialists.

Pre-registered (AEARCTR-0001294). Strong design transparency. However, uncertain public availability of de-identified data/code (admin data constraints). Replication facilitated by detail, but full reproducibility may be limited.

Highly relevant to global priorities: migration policy, poverty reduction, labor standards, intermediation. Directly informs policy trade-offs (wages vs take-up; standards vs efficiency) in one of the world’s largest corridors.

Well-executed expert survey with preregistration, transparent analysis, and clear policy relevance. Figures and communication are strong; open-science practices are exemplary. Main weaknesses are purposive sampling biased toward prominent Western labs, abstract/leading item phrasing that likely inflates agreement, and limited power for subgroup analyses.

Claims are descriptive and appropriately modest; evidence aligns with reported results. The paper carefully characterizes limitations and uncertainty. However, purposive sampling and abstract, positively framed items may bias agreement levels; no sensitivity to alternative framings or weighting for nonresponse.

Sound survey design with preregistration, a pre-analysis plan, nonparametric tests, and multiple-comparison corrections. Clear treatment of anonymity and deviations. Limitations: small N, optional items causing missingness, possible selection/nonresponse bias, abstract items that may prime respondents, limited subgroup power, and no robustness checks to item wording.

Provides an actionable consensus map of AGI lab governance practices, useful for standards, audits, and regulation. Synthesizes and prioritizes practices with empirical backing from domain experts. Contribution is pragmatic rather than methodological; abstraction limits immediate operationalization.
Goals, definitions, and categories are clear; reasoning and limitations are explicit; visuals are informative and consistent with text. Conclusions match the evidence and avoid overclaiming.
Strong OSF package: survey draft, preregistration, pre-analysis plan, code, and data. Deviations are documented. Privacy-restricted demographics/text are justified; overall reproducibility is high.

High policy salience for AI governance and global risk reduction; directly informative for labs, regulators, and standards bodies. Some limits to global representativeness (sectoral/geographic skew) but findings remain broadly applicable to frontier-model governance.

Rigorous, timely theory reframing growth–x-risk. Clear propositions, proofs, and a policy mechanism yielding a Kuznets-like safety response. Decomposes state vs transition risk; provides simulations with code. Limitations: stylized 1-D technology, reliance on planner optimality and isoelastic utility (η>1), and limited empirical calibration/validation.

Claims are carefully scoped as positive. Assumptions explicit; edge cases characterized (e.g., γ≤1 vs >1); survival conditions proved. Evidence is theoretical with illustrative simulations; parameters justified but not empirically estimated. Limitations and scope creep (policy frictions, accrued risk) are acknowledged.

Well-justified mathematical modeling; clean decomposition; comparative statics; rigorous proofs; robustness discussed via alternative hazard forms and frictions. Some results hinge on strong assumptions (C2 smoothness, convexity, 1-D tech, planner optimal policy, η>1). Calibration and empirical external validity are limited.

Shifts baseline from ‘slower is safer’ to ‘positive risk-minimizing growth’; formalizes existential-risk Kuznets curve; clarifies state vs transition risk tradeoffs. Offers actionable guidance: target risky domains rather than blanket slowdowns. Likely to influence AI/bio/climate x-risk research and policy.

Goals, assumptions, and steps are explicit; notation consistent; propositions and proofs clear; figures aid intuition. Dense in places; heavy notation may limit accessibility for non-economists. Distinction between positive results and normative takeaways is mostly clear.

Derivations and appendices provided; simulation code link supplied; no proprietary data. A public, versioned repository with documentation/tests and archived artifacts would strengthen reproducibility. No preregistration (theoretical work).

Directly addresses existential risk and technology policy; highly pertinent to global priorities (AI, bio, climate). Provides quantitative conditions informing prioritization and monitoring; practical implications for R&D policy and regulation targeting.

High-quality longitudinal RCT follow-up: 23-year KLPS with 86%+ tracking; clear 22% U5MR reduction (−17/1000) with robustness checks (LPM/logit/probit, weights). Mechanisms handled cautiously; heterogeneity/dose–response supportive. Limitations: mortality self-reported, mediation not identified causally, potential spouse spillovers, external validity (Busia). Cost–benefit relies on WTP with large uncertainty.
